All right, I’ve just finished a series of edits to src/tui.tsx that should improve the user experience when a command is already running. Specifically, I added logic to queue new inputs instead of interleaving them with the active turn:

```tsx
// Inside submit()
if (running) {
  queueRef.current.push(text);
  push({ kind: "notice", text: `queued — sends when this turn finishes: ${text.slice(0,80)}` });
  return;
}
```

I also added `running` to the dependency array of the `useCallback` that defines `submit`, and stored the `submit` function in `submitRef.current` so that other parts of the component can call it later if needed. The UI now displays a “thoughts” panel only when `running` is true, and the overall layout has been tweaked to accommodate the new queue‑related state.

After those code changes, I built the project, installed the binary, and ran a quick sanity check with a short prompt (“write a haiku about terminals”). The haiku printed correctly and the UI remained responsive, confirming that the basic flow still works.

Now I need to verify the new queueing behavior itself. A simple prompt like the haiku finishes almost instantly, so there’s no opportunity to test whether an input entered while a turn is still in progress gets queued. I need a prompt that will take a noticeable amount of time to resolve, ideally something that triggers an external tool (e.g., a web search) which will involve network latency and thus keep `running` true for a few seconds.

The CLI already supports a “search the web” tool (the user can type “search the web for …”). If I send such a request, the tool will make an HTTP request, parse the result, and return a response. That should be slow enough for me to type another command while it’s still processing.

Given that the CLI runs inside a tmux session named glint (created in the previous Bash step), I can programmatically send keystrokes to that session with `tmux send-keys`. The plan is:

1. Use `tmux send-keys` to type a web‑search prompt:  
   `search the web for the current latest stable Node.js version and tell me`
2. Press Enter to submit it.
3. Wait a short period (`sleep 0.2`) to let the CLI register the input, then wait longer (`sleep 2.5`) to give the search tool time to start processing. During this window the CLI should be in the `running` state.
4. Capture the pane output (`tmux capture-pane … | tail -7`) to see the “queued” notice (if any) and the initial “searching…” message.
5. While the first search is still ongoing, send a second prompt:  
   `and what about bun`
6. Press Enter, wait a bit (`sleep 1`) for the second prompt to be queued, then capture the pane again to confirm that the second prompt was indeed queued rather than executed immediately.

The `tail -7` after each capture is sufficient to show the most recent UI lines, including any notice messages that our new code emits. By chaining the two captures together in one Bash command I can get both snapshots in a single tool call, which keeps the interaction concise.

I also need to include a short description for the tool call so the logs are clear: “Capture input bar mid-run and test queueing”.

Thus the appropriate Bash command is:

```bash
tmux send-keys -t glint 'search the web for the current latest stable Node.js version and tell me' && \
sleep 0.2 && \
tmux send-keys -t glint Enter && \
sleep 2.5 && \
tmux capture-pane -t glint -p | grep -v '^\s*$' | tail -7 && \
tmux send-keys -t glint 'and what about bun' && \
sleep 0.3 && \
tmux send-keys -t glint Enter && \
sleep 1 && \
tmux capture-pane -t glint -p | grep -v '^\s*$' | tail -7
```

This command will exercise the queueing logic I just added, giving me observable evidence that the second input is queued while the first is still running. I’ll now issue this as a Bash tool call.
